findings.title: Hung spawn flushers are never killed, so restarts overlap
findings.body: Workers are created with multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process, i.e. SpawnProcess. That class subclasses multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess, not multiprocessing.Process, so isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) is always false for real flusher processes. The new guard therefore never calls kill() in _ensure_processes_alive, and the same check in join() never calls terminate(). Previously kill() was unconditional, so this is a regression on the default single-process path as well as the multi-process path. A hung worker is left running, the restart counter is incremented, and _create_process_for_shards overwrites self.processes and drops the only reference the strategy keeps. The orphan keeps calling flush_segments/produce/done_flush_segments on the same shards as the replacement, which can duplicate segments on the buffered-segments topic or delete Redis state the other worker is still producing. The replacement also resets process_healthy_since, so once it looks healthy the parent stops retrying and the orphan runs until the consumer process exits. join() likewise cannot SIGTERM a worker blocked in Redis or Kafka that never observes the stopped flag. Thread-mode restarts (produce_to_pipe) leak the same way because nothing stops the previous thread. Even after the type check is fixed (use BaseProcess, or skip only threading.Thread), kill() is asynchronous and the replacement is started immediately with no join; the old worker must be reaped before a new one is started.

findings.title: Timed join returns while flusher processes are still running
findings.body: join() sets a deadline, spends the full timeout in next_step.join(timeout), then walks flusher workers. If the deadline is already exhausted it breaks immediately; if it expires mid-loop the break skips every remaining worker. Those workers are neither waited on nor terminated. close() intentionally does not stop flushers (to avoid a Redis memory spike at rebalance start), so join() is the only shutdown barrier. A worker blocked in flush_segments or Kafka produce will not see stopped until that call returns, and after the break nothing signals it. Kafka rebalance then builds a new SpanFlusher for the same shards — in this process or another — while the old workers are still flushing, so both produce the same segments and race on Redis flush markers. The previous single-process join always fell through to terminate() after the wait; the early break is a regression. On the way out of join(), every worker that is still alive must be killed and joined, including when the timeout is already spent.

findings.title: test_basic wait is a no-op, so the flush assertion is racy
findings.body: test_basic monkeypatches time.sleep to a no-op, then after setting fac._flusher.current_drift calls time.sleep(0.1) to let the flusher thread observe the new clock. That call is the patched no-op, so it does not wait, and the extra step.poll() does not flush either: SpanFlusher.poll only forwards to the committer while flushing runs on the background thread. step.join() then sets the shared stopped flag before it waits for the thread. If the thread has not yet read the updated drift, it sees stopped and exits without producing, and (msg,) = messages fails. The race is intermittent and worse under CI load. Wait with a sleep that was bound before the patch, or poll messages until the payload appears, using a real timeout.

findings.title: Flusher metric tag is comma-joined and inconsistently keyed
findings.body: shard_tag is ','.join of every shard id on the process and is sent as the shard tag on spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes. spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce uses a different key, shards, so it will not line up with those series or with spans.buffer.flusher_unhealthy, which tags a single shard id. With the CLI default --flusher-processes 1 the value is the consumer's whole partition assignment (for example 0,1,2,...,N). DogStatsD/statsd tag lists are comma-separated, so a comma inside the value is parsed as extra tags and the timer is dropped or recorded as a truncated series such as shard:0. Rebalances also mint a new series per assignment, which is unbounded cardinality. Emit one shard id per point (or omit the tag when shards are grouped) and use the same key on all three metrics.
